article.title: Extension functions in C++/PHP
article.p: This section describes how to extend the capability of Saxon XSLT stylesheets and XQuery queries by adding user written extension functions in the C++, Python and PHP languages.

Extension functions allow code written in a host programming language such as C++ to be invoked directly from a function call in an XPath expression (whether in XSLT, XQuery, or pure XPath). For this to work the Saxon processor needs to be able to locate the executable code corresponding to a particular function name. For the function arguments these can be as XDM types or converted to the host language type system, with the opposite conversion applied to the function result.

XSLT, XQuery, and XPath are functional languages where it is assumed that functions do not have side effects. Saxon cannot stop you calling extension functions that have side effects, but the effect of doing so is not always guaranteed. For example, the optimizer might eliminate a call to an extension function whose results are never used, or it might execute calls to extension functions in an unexpected order.

Allowing untrusted stylesheets or queries to call extension functions is a potential security risk. Stylesheets and queries will only be able to call extension functions that have been explicitly registered by the application; it is the responsibility of the application designer to ensure that this does not create vulnerabilities.

To register a user defined function SaxonC needs to know the signature of any function that it might call. The signature tells the processor the name of each function that can be called, the number and types pf its arguments. and the expected return type.
SaxonC provides a new API for registering extension functions. This registration must be done before any attempt is made to evaluate an expression or compile an XSLT stylesheet that uses one.

The SaxonProcessor class in the SaxonC API contains for this purpose the registerUserFunction(apiDescription) method, which takes a JSON string of the user's function. This method exists on the C++, Python and PHP APIs for SaxonC.
The apiDescription argument is a map of the following form:
The namespace identifies the function namespace, the signature for the function. The local name of the function identifies the function name; each signature has four properties:

tr.td: The return type, an XML Schema data type, for example xs:boolean.
The parameter types, one for each parameter, as an XML Schema data type.

The function arities. In the common case, this is just an array of length one containing the arity of the function. If the function can be called with multiple arities, this is a list of the arities that can be used, for example [1, 3, 4] for a function that can be called with one, three, or four arguments.

article.p: When compiling a stylesheet (with the SaxonC EE compiler), the registered extension functions are provided in a JSON object using SaxonProcessor.registerUserFunction(apiDescription).
article.h2: Function argument and return type conversions
article.p: As mentioned above, when an XDM item is passed to the user function in the host language (i.e. C++, PHP or Python), it can be passed as an XDM type or for Python and PHP the item can be converted into the Python or PHP representation, respectively. Conversely, when a function wants to return a value, it can either be returned as an XDM type or a Python/PHP representation that can be converted back into an XDM type. We discuss these in more detail for each host language in SaxonC.
For general information about extension functions, see Extension functions.
To write extension functions in C++, see Extension functions (C++).
To write extension functions in PHP, see Extension functions (PHP).
To write extension functions in Python, see Extension functions (Python).

section.title: Writing extension functions in C++
section.p: A full example of the use of extension functions can be found in the files testXPath.cpp in the samples/cppTest directory. This sample test registers a user written C++ extension function called "myFunc". Arguments and return types of User functions written in C++ can only be XDM types. This is different to Python and PHP which can handle native types.

Example C++ code to register user function:
processor->registerUserFunction("http://www.example.com", &myFunc, "{ \"myFunc\": {" " \"as\": \"xs:integer?\"," " \"param\": [" " \"xs:integer\"" " ]," " \"arity\": [1]" " }" "}");

Notice in the registration of the user function in C++ that we pass the function as a void pointer to the registerUserFunction method. This is essential for the call-back mechanism. The arguments must also have the signature (int length, XdmValue*). Where length is the number of arguments being passed to the function from the SaxonC processor. section.title: Writing extension functions in PHP
section.p: An example of the use of extension functions can be found in the sample file xsltExamples.php in the samples/php directory. The example registers a user written PHP extension function called "userFunction", which is then called from an XSLT stylesheet by calling the php:function() function.
section.h2: Calling extension functions from XSLT and XQuery
section.p: User written PHP extension functions can be called from XSLT and XQuery by using the php:function() function. This is a Saxon extension function in a special namespace ("http://php.net/xsl"), which takes two arguments: the function name, as an xs:string, and the arguments to the function, supplied as an XDM array.
